name: Museum of Fine Arts
description: Hungary's principal art museum, housed since 1906 in a neoclassical building on Heroes' Square. Its collections range from Egyptian antiquities and Greek and Roman art to Old Master paintings by Raphael, El Greco and Goya, sculpture, drawings and prints, shown alongside temporary exhibitions.

children.text: The Museum of Fine Arts, Szépművészeti Múzeum, is described by Finestre sull'Arte as the largest art museum in Hungary. It stands on Heroes' Square facing the Műcsarnok exhibition hall, and its holdings are organised into departments including Egyptian antiquities, classical antiquities, Old Master paintings, sculpture, graphics and art after 1800. Figures vary by source, but the collection runs to well over a hundred thousand works.

The decision to found the museum was made in 1896, and the site chosen was the square in front of the Műcsarnok. Albert Schickedanz and Fülöp Herzog designed both buildings, and the museum's eclectic neoclassical building was built between 1900 and 1906. It opened on 1 December 1906 in the presence of Emperor Franz Joseph, and the public could enter from 5 December. Its origins lie in collections from noble Hungarian families such as the Esterházy, Pyrker, Ipolyi and Jankovich, which the state acquired in the late nineteenth century.

The Old Master paintings number about three thousand and include Raphael's Esterházy Madonna, Correggio's Madonna of the Milk and works by Titian, Giorgione, Tintoretto, Dürer, Rubens, El Greco, Velázquez and Goya. The Egyptian collection includes painted mummy sarcophagi, and the classical collection includes 135 marble works acquired from Paul Arndt in 1908. Drawings and prints are shown in rotating exhibitions. A Giorgione painting was stolen in 1983 and recovered in Greece in 1984.

The twentieth century left its mark. The building was bombed in the Second World War, and part of the collection was taken to Germany. Works recovered in 1946 and 1947 were often damaged, and We Love Budapest notes that works taken by the Red Army remain in Russian museums. In 1957 the Hungarian artworks moved to the new Hungarian National Gallery, and the two institutions were reunited in 2012.

The museum closed on 15 February 2015 for a renovation led by the Mányi Studio. Its main aim was to restore the Romanesque Hall, which had been a storeroom for decades. Check the official museum site for the current galleries and exhibitions rather than relying on older reports.
Good to know
Heroes' Square and the Műcsarnok are directly beside the museum, so they combine naturally in one visit.
Check the official museum site for current opening times, tickets and temporary exhibitions before you go.
The collection is large; choose two or three departments, such as the Old Masters or the Egyptian collection, rather than trying to see everything.
The Romanesque Hall was restored as part of the museum's renovation; check which galleries are currently on show.

historyIntro: The Museum of Fine Arts anchors Heroes' Square with a collection that puts Budapest's artistic identity in a wider European and ancient-world context.

children.text: The museum was established in the era when Budapest's public institutions were growing rapidly around the Millennium Monument. Its monumental classical-style building faces Heroes' Square, alongside the Kunsthalle exhibition hall.

historySections.heading: Collections from Egypt to European painting

children.text: The museum now brings together ancient Egyptian and classical objects, old masters and later works. Its historic and modern galleries allow visitors to follow contrasting artistic traditions rather than only Hungarian painting.

name: Andrássy Avenue
description: Andrássy Avenue is Pest's grand boulevard, laid out in the 1870s to link the inner city with City Park. Lined with Neo-Renaissance palaces and built over the Millennium Underground, it runs past the Opera House and the Oktogon to Heroes' Square and forms part of Budapest's UNESCO World Heritage listing.

children.text: Andrássy Avenue is the long, tree-lined boulevard that links the inner city of Pest with City Park. It was decreed in 1870 to relieve traffic on the parallel Király utca and to connect the centre with the park. Construction began in 1872, and the avenue was inaugurated on 20 August 1876. It was named after Gyula Andrássy, the Prime Minister described as the main supporter of the plan, in 1885 or 1886 depending on the source, and most of the palaces along it were finished by 1884.

The layout blended proposals from three competitors: Lajos Lechner, Frigyes Feszl, and the firm Klein and Fraser. The palaces were designed by leading architects of the day, led by Miklós Ybl. A summary of the UNESCO listing says that from 1872 the avenue radically transformed the urban structure of Pest. It is part of the World Heritage Site Budapest, including the Banks of the Danube, the Buda Castle Quarter and Andrássy Avenue, which was extended to include it in 2002.

Under the avenue runs the Millennium Underground Railway, today Line M1 of the Budapest Metro. It was built in 1894-1896 and is described as the first underground railway in continental Europe. It opened on 2 May 1896 with its southern terminus at Vörösmarty Square, to carry visitors to the millennium celebrations in the Városliget. The avenue's outer end is Heroes' Square, which belongs to the same heritage listing.

Notable buildings along the avenue include the State Opera House, the former Ballet School, the Zoltán Kodály Memorial Museum and Archives, the Hungarian University of Fine Arts and the Ferenc Hopp Museum of Asiatic Arts. Other landmarks include the House of Terror and the Oktogon junction. A Budappest feature on the avenue's 150th anniversary also mentions Kodály Körönd and Liszt Ferenc Square as places along the route.

The avenue's name has changed with politics. It became Stalin Street in 1950, was briefly called the Avenue of Hungarian Youth during the 1956 uprising, was renamed People's Republic Street in 1957, and regained the name Andrássy út in 1990. The year 2026 is the 150th anniversary of its inauguration.
Good to know
Use the M1 metro to ride under the avenue, or walk the route on the surface to look at the palace facades above street level.
The avenue ends at Heroes' Square beside City Park, so it works well as a one-direction walk with the metro for the return.
Check the official sites of the Opera House, the House of Terror and the Hopp Museum for visiting details, since each has its own arrangements.

historyIntro: Andrássy Avenue tells the story of how nineteenth-century Budapest designed a capital with imperial-scale ambitions and a distinctive public life.

children.text: Created during the city's great period of expansion, the avenue connected the central streets with the developing City Park. Its broad urban design supported prestigious residences, public institutions and an increasingly fashionable cultural district.

The Hungarian State Opera and later grand villas mark different stretches of the avenue. The Millennium Underground Railway, built for the 1896 festivities, runs beneath the corridor, making architecture and transport part of the same historical route.

name: Váci Street
description: Váci Street is the pedestrian street running south from Vörösmarty Square, long a shopping and promenading route in downtown Pest. It takes its name from the road to Vác, has a mixed German, Greek and Serbian past after 1686, and carries a mix of historic facades, souvenir shops and cafés.

children.text: Váci utca is a central pedestrian street in downtown Pest, running south from Vörösmarty Square. Wikipedia describes it as one of the city's main pedestrian thoroughfares and often called the most famous in the city, with many restaurants and shops aimed at visitors. Its name refers to the road to the town of Vác; a walking article on We Love Budapest adds that a gate stood between numbers 2 and 3 until it was demolished in 1789, when the street was lengthened and Vörösmarty Square created.

After the Ottomans were expelled in 1686, the Habsburgs shaped the street, joining land behind the Downtown Abbey with the remains of an older Ottoman street. They sold plots mainly to imperial Germans, Greeks and Serbs, with some Jewish buyers, so the street was not typically Hungarian, and most shop signs were in German until the late eighteenth century. A 1911 arrangement with the Piarists, who were rebuilding their school at number 27, required a pedestrian alley to connect through to Elisabeth Bridge.

The street rewards looking up. The We Love Budapest walk points to the Pesti Theater at number 9, the Hungarian Crown at number 14, a carved wooden gate at number 15, a half-cut Pegasus at number 20, the Harris Bazaar at number 34, the Officers' Casino at number 38, a plaque marking a Swedish king's visit at number 43, and the Serbian House at number 66. Wikipedia mentions that the shop Alter és Kiss was founded by Antal Alter in 1829 at number 10, now number 13. Some buildings were bombed in the wars and later rebuilt.

Today the street is a place for souvenirs, shopping and eating, and for a stroll south from Vörösmarty Square. Wikipedia also warns that some bars along the street are known for clip joints, where tourists are lured in and then charged heavily for drinks, so it is sensible to check a menu and its prices before you sit down.
Good to know
Start at Vörösmarty Square, where the M1 metro line has its southern terminus, and walk south along the pedestrian street.
Look above the shop windows for the older facades and house numbers mentioned in walking guides.
Check menus and prices before sitting in any bar or restaurant, and avoid anyone inviting you in off the street.
Since shop hours vary, check each shop's own page for current opening times.

heroImage.alt: Crowds and café terraces on pedestrian Váci Street in the evening

historyIntro: Váci Street is a busy pedestrian route, but beneath the shops lies the memory of an older commercial Pest shaped by trade and changing city life.

historySections.heading: From historic street to shopping promenade

children.text: The street belongs to Pest's long-established urban centre. As Budapest modernised, commercial façades, cafés and stores gave the route a central place in the city's public life. Architectural details from different periods survive above contemporary shopfronts.

Today the street joins squares, restaurants and side lanes rather than functioning as a single monument. Its seasonal decorations and street activity reflect the continued role of the centre as a place for promenading, trade and encounters.

name: New York Café
description: A Belle Époque coffeehouse on the ground floor of the former New York Life Insurance building on the Grand Boulevard. Its frescoed ceilings, gilded stucco and sixteen carved fauns draw visitors, and for decades writers and poets treated it as an informal office. Today it sits inside a hotel.

children.text: The New York Café occupies the ground floor of what was built as the Budapest office of the New York Life Insurance Company, at Erzsébet körút 9-11 on the Grand Boulevard. Wikipedia gives the opening date of the building as 23 October 1894 and names Alajos Hauszmann, Flóris Korb and Kálmán Giergl as its architects. The company's name explains the name of the café, and the building is now the Anantara New York Palace Budapest Hotel.

The café became known for its interior, which visitors describe as frescoed ceilings, gilded stucco panels, marble columns and large chandeliers. Wikipedia credits the sculptor Károly Senyei with the statues and ornaments of the facade and with the café's sixteen devilish fauns. It also describes the café as a longtime centre of Hungarian literature and poetry, and a travel guide notes that writers used it as an informal office for working, meeting colleagues and finding patrons.

The twentieth century was less kind. The building was damaged in the Second World War and later nationalised under communism. In 1954 the café was renamed the Hungaria Café, and in 1957 the sculptors Sándor Boldogfai Farkas, Ödön Metky and János Sóváry carved replicas of the damaged allegorical sculptures, among them figures of Thrift and Wealth and of America and Hungary. The café regained its New York name in 1989, after the fall of communism.

In early 2001 the Hungarian government sold the building to the Italian hotel group Boscolo, and after a complete renovation it reopened as a hotel on 5 May 2006 with the restored café. The hotel changed names several times and has been called Anantara New York Palace Budapest since November 2021. For visitors, the café is on the Grand Boulevard near Blaha Lujza tér, and because it sits inside a hotel it is worth confirming current access and any booking arrangements on the official site.
Good to know
Metro line M2 and trams 4 and 6 are listed by one guide as the way to reach the area around Blaha Lujza tér on the Grand Boulevard.
Look up at the ceilings and for the carved fauns, which Wikipedia attributes to Károly Senyei.
The café is part of a hotel, so check the official site for current opening times, access and any reservation rules.

historyIntro: New York Café is a reminder that Budapest's grand coffeehouses were once important meeting places for journalists, writers and cultural life.

historySections.heading: An ornate café in a growing metropolis

children.text: The café opened within the New York Palace at the end of the nineteenth century. Elaborate ceilings, gilding and large mirrors gave it the kind of theatrical interior that made Budapest's café culture famous.

Coffeehouses became social workplaces where editors and writers exchanged ideas over long afternoons. The palace's story also reflects twentieth-century changes of use and later restoration, which returned the interior to its current lavish appearance.
